title: Greek Ionia
subtitle: 1,050–494 BC · Miletus, Ephesus and the First Philosophers, from the Ionian Migration to the Revolt

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The twelve cities and their league, the tyrants of Miletus and Samos, and the lords of Lydia and Persia

entries.label: The Ionian migration
entries.hint: Later Greeks said that the Ionians left Attica after the Dorian invasion under sons of King Codrus, and founded twelve cities on the central coast of Asia Minor, mixing with the Carians and Lelegians they found there. The archaeology shows Greek Protogeometric pottery on the coast from about 1000 BC and no clean break with the Late Bronze Age settlements. The 'migration' was a long, mixed process, later told as a single founding.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.142–147; Pausanias 7.2–4; Strabo 14.1.3; Peter Ruggieri and Jonathan Hall on Ionian origins.

entries.label: The Panionion and the twelve cities
entries.hint: Twelve cities — Miletus, Myus, Priene, Ephesus, Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Clazomenae, Phocaea, Erythrae, Chios and Samos — shared a sanctuary of Poseidon Helikonios on Mount Mykale called the Panionion, and gathered there each year for a festival and for common business. Smyrna later joined the group. The league had a shared cult and a shared identity but never became a state.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.142–148, 1.149–150 (Smyrna); Hans Lohmann on the Mykale sanctuary (excavations from 2004), identification debated.

entries.label: Thrasybulus of Miletus
entries.hint: Thrasybulus, tyrant of Miletus when Alyattes of Lydia made war on the city, ended the siege by a ruse: when Alyattes' envoy arrived, he had all the stored grain brought into the agora and the city feasted, so the Lydian king, thinking the siege was no use, made peace and an alliance. Miletus came out of the Lydian wars with its independence and a guest-friendship with Lydia.

entries.label: Polycrates of Samos
entries.hint: With his brothers, Polycrates seized Samos at a festival of Hera, then ruled alone, with a fleet of a hundred penteconters, a mercenary force, and a court that welcomed Anacreon. His power over the Aegean was famous and ended when the Persian satrap Oroetes lured him to the mainland and had him crucified. His Samos built the tunnel, the harbour mole and the temple.

entries.label: Croesus and the Ionian cities
entries.hint: Croesus was the first foreigner to subject Greek cities on the coast. The Ephesians surrendered and he made their tyrant Pindarus, his own nephew, step down. The other Ionian and Aeolian cities were made to pay tribute but were left self-governing, in return for which Croesus gave gifts to the Artemision and Didyma.

entries.label: The Persian governors and the tyrants
entries.hint: After Cyrus took Sardis, the cities were ruled from Sardis by the Persian satrap and, in the cities, by local tyrants who held power by Persian favour. They paid a fixed tribute and supplied ships and soldiers to the king. They found themselves, in time, fighting for the Great King as far as the Danube and Scythia.

entries.label: Histiaios and Aristagoras of Miletus
entries.hint: Histiaios was rewarded for guarding the Danube bridge with land in Thrace, then kept at Susa as an adviser to Darius. His kinsman Aristagoras ruled Miletus in his place, tried a failed campaign at Naxos with Persian backing, and, to avoid blame, led the cities into revolt. Both men died away from Miletus.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Cimmerian raiders, the Lydian wars, the Persian conquest and the Ionian Revolt that ended in Miletus's fall

entries.label: The Cimmerian raids
entries.hint: Cimmerian horsemen raided the Ionian coast around the middle of the seventh century. Magnesia on the Maeander was destroyed and, according to a later hymn, they threatened the sanctuary of Artemis at Ephesus. The poet Archilochus is cited for the fall of Magnesia.
entries.note: Archilochus fr. 20 West (via Strabo 14.1.40); Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis 251–258.

entries.label: Alyattes' war on Miletus
entries.hint: Lydian armies invaded the Milesian territory each year for eleven years, burning crops but never taking the city, which was provisioned by sea. When the wars ended in a treaty, the Milesians were allies of Lydia. The war was a series of raids and a siege rather than battles.

entries.label: Alyattes takes Smyrna
entries.hint: Alyattes of Lydia sacked Smyrna, which the Colophonians had taken from the Aeolians and made a member of the Ionian group. The city, a village from then on for four centuries, was rebuilt only under Alexander's successors. Alyattes' attack on Clazomenae failed.

entries.label: Harpagus conquers the Ionian cities
entries.hint: After Cyrus took Sardis, Harpagus subdued the cities one by one, using siege mounds. Phocaea's people sailed away to Corsica, and those of Teos abandoned their city for Thrace; the Milesians, who had made terms with Cyrus, were untouched. The Ionians' appeal to Sparta produced only a diplomatic message.

entries.label: The burning of Sardis
entries.hint: Ionian and Athenian troops marched inland, surprised Sardis and set it on fire, the temple of Cybele included, then were caught on their way back by the Persians and routed at Ephesus. Darius, it is said, asked who the Athenians were and ordered a servant to remind him of them at dinner thrice a day.

entries.label: Lade and the fall of Miletus
entries.hint: The Ionian fleet of some 350 ships met the Persian and Phoenician fleet at Lade off Miletus; many of the Samian ships sailed away and the line broke. Miletus was taken and sacked, the Didyma sanctuary burned, and the men were killed and the women and children enslaved. It was the end of the Ionian Revolt.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A federal plan, the arbitration of Miletus, a people's council on Chios and the Persian land survey

entries.label: The people's council of Chios
entries.hint: An inscribed stone from Chios, among the earliest Greek political documents, regulates the work of a 'people's council' (demosie boule) of fifty men from each tribe, an appeal against officials' judgments and fines. It shows an island state with a developed system of councils and legal appeals a century before Athens' reforms.
entries.note: Meiggs and Lewis, Greek Historical Inscriptions no. 8 (Chian constitutional inscription).

entries.label: Thales's federal proposal
entries.hint: When the Persians threatened, the philosopher Thales advised the Ionians to set up a single deliberative council at Teos, in the middle of the cities, with each city treated as a deme. The plan was never adopted, but it is the earliest recorded Greek proposal for a federal state.

entries.label: The first satrapy and its tribute
entries.hint: In Darius's organisation of the empire the Ionians, Magnesians, Aeolians, Carians, Lycians, Milyans and Pamphylians formed the first tribute district, paying 400 talents of silver a year. The Ionian cities were taxed as one group by the satrap at Sardis, with the cities responsible for their own collection.

entries.label: The Parians settle Miletus
entries.hint: Torn by civil strife for two generations, the Milesians invited ten citizens of Paros to put the city in order. The Parians toured the countryside, noted which farms were well kept, and made the owners of those the government of the city. The story is a rare picture of an external arbitrator and an idea of civic office as tied to competence in managing land.

entries.label: Artaphernes' land survey
entries.hint: After the revolt the satrap Artaphernes had the territory of each city measured in parasangs and set the tribute accordingly, which came out at about the same as before. Mardonius the next year put down the tyrants and set up democracies. Persian policy was to restore order by rule, not terror.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Panionion, the Artemision of Ephesus and the oracle of Didyma

entries.label: The Panionia — a festival for all Ionians
entries.hint: Each year the twelve cities sent delegates and sacrifices to the Panionion for the Panionia, a festival of Poseidon Helikonios, a god of earthquake and sea. Later writers say the Ionians of Asia continued the sacrifices after the others had ended. The festival expressed an identity that had political force only in crises.

entries.label: Artemis of Ephesus
entries.hint: The Artemision at Ephesus was a shrine of an Anatolian goddess of fertility, merged with the Greek Artemis, whose cult image bore rows of rounded forms on her chest. By around 560 BC it had grown into the great dipteral temple, largely of marble, with columns funded by Croesus. The cult drew visitors, treasure and asylum-seekers from across the Aegean.
entries.note: David Hogarth, Excavations at Ephesus (1908); Anton Bammer on the Artemision; Herodotus 1.92.

entries.label: The oracle of Apollo at Didyma
entries.hint: South of Miletus, the oracle of Apollo at Didyma was run by a hereditary clan, the Branchidae, and was consulted by Croesus and by Pharaoh Necho, who dedicated his dress there. Its sixth-century temple was a vast Ionic building. The Persians burned the sanctuary after Lade, and the Branchidae are said to have been moved away to Sogdiana.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Homer's cities, the lyric poets, the Ionic temple and the korai of Samos

entries.label: Homer's Ionia
entries.hint: The Iliad and the Odyssey are in an Ionic dialect with Aeolic elements and were attributed in antiquity to Homer of Smyrna or of Chios. A Chian guild of rhapsodes, the Homeridae, claimed him as ancestor, and the Hymn to Apollo says that the blind poet lived in rocky Chios. The epics were shaped by the Ionian coast, whatever the poet's name.
entries.note: Homeric Hymn to Apollo 172–173; Strabo 14.1.37; Martin West, The Making of the Iliad (2011).

entries.label: The Ionians' festival at Delos
entries.hint: The Homeric Hymn to Apollo pictures the Ionians gathering at Delos with their wives and children, with boxing, dance and song, and the maidens of Delos who sing hymns of Apollo, Leto and Artemis and can imitate the voices of all men. It is the oldest account of a Greek festival in which choral song and dance were the center.

entries.label: Mimnermus, Hipponax and Anacreon
entries.hint: Ionia gave the lyric poets of love, abuse and wine: Mimnermus of Colophon with his short elegies on youth and old age, Hipponax of Ephesus with his limping iambics and the coarse language of the street, and Anacreon of Teos, who sang at the courts of Polycrates and the Pisistratids.
entries.note: Fragments of Mimnermus, Hipponax, Anacreon (West, Iambi et Elegi Graeci; Page, Poetae Melici Graeci).

entries.label: The Ionic temple
entries.hint: In the sixth century the Ionians created the Ionic order, with slim columns, volute capitals and a continuous frieze, in the giant dipteral temples of Hera on Samos and Artemis at Ephesus. The Samos temple, by Rhoikos and Theodoros, was by Herodotus's reckoning the largest he had seen. The order later marked half of Greek architecture.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.60; Vitruvius 3.2 and 7 (preface); Hans Walter on the Samian Heraion.

entries.label: The Samian korai and kouroi
entries.hint: Samos produced the earliest large marble figures of draped girls (korai) and young men, in a language of columnar bodies, full cheeks and intricate drapery, among them the kore dedicated by a man named Cheramyes and the monumental family group dedicated by Geneleos. The sculptures show what the Ionian workshops did with Egyptian and eastern models.
entries.note: Cheramyes Kore (Louvre Ma 686); Geneleos group (Samos Museum); Hans Walter and Helmut Kyrieleis on the Heraion finds.

entries.label: The Capture of Miletus
entries.hint: Phrynichus's tragedy on the fall of Miletus so moved the Athenian audience to tears that the city fined him a thousand drachmas for reminding them of their own misfortunes and forbade any future performance. It is the first known tragedy on a contemporary event, and shows how deeply Athens identified with its Ionian kin.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Thales, Anaximander, Anaximenes, Hecataeus, Heraclitus, Xenophanes and Pythagoras

entries.label: Thales of Miletus
entries.hint: Thales was said to have predicted a solar eclipse, which in 585 BC stopped a battle between the Lydians and the Medes, and to have held that water is the origin of all things. Whatever the details, he is the first Greek to seek the cause of natural events in nature itself rather than in the acts of gods, and with him the philosophical tradition begins.

entries.label: Anaximander and the boundless
entries.hint: Anaximander of Miletus wrote the first prose work on nature, with the boundless (apeiron) as the source of things, an earth suspended in space without support and animals that came from the sea. He is also credited with a map of the known world and a gnomon sundial.
entries.note: Anaximander fr. 1 (Simplicius, in Physica 24.13); Agathemerus 1.1; Diogenes Laertius 2.1–2.

entries.label: Anaximenes and air
entries.hint: Anaximenes took air as the source of all things and explained how it could become fire by rarefaction and wind, cloud, water, earth and stone by condensation. His account tries to make change a matter of quantity — the first physical mechanism in Greek thought.

entries.label: Xenophanes of Colophon
entries.hint: After the Persian conquest, Xenophanes left Colophon and wandered the Greek world as a rhapsode, mocking Homer and Hesiod for their stories of gods that steal and commit adultery. He said that if horses had hands they would draw gods like horses, and that there was one god, unlike mortals in body or mind.
entries.note: Xenophanes fragments (DK 21), esp. B11, B15, B23.

entries.label: Pythagoras of Samos
entries.hint: Pythagoras left Samos around 530 BC, in the later years of Polycrates' rule, and settled in Croton in southern Italy, where he founded a brotherhood of religious and political discipline, studied number and harmony and taught the transmigration of souls. The tradition is tangled with later legend.
entries.note: Diogenes Laertius 8.1–50; Porphyry, Life of Pythagoras; Walter Burkert, Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972).

entries.label: Hecataeus of Miletus
entries.hint: Hecataeus wrote the Circuit of the Earth, a geography with a corrected map, and the Genealogies, which began by saying that the stories of the Greeks were many and ridiculous. His work shows historical criticism applied to local tradition, and he advised the Ionians in the revolt, urging them to build a fleet and to take the treasure of Didyma.

entries.label: Heraclitus of Ephesus
entries.hint: Heraclitus wrote in riddling prose that the world is a flux ruled by a hidden logos and by the strife of opposites, that one cannot step twice into the same river, and that fire is the stuff of the world's change. His book was said to have been deposited in the temple of Artemis, and he held the many in contempt.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Electrum coins, Chian wine and Milesian wool

entries.label: The silting of the gulf
entries.hint: The Maeander river brought silt down to the Latmian Gulf, and its delta moved west over the centuries. Miletus's four harbours were silted over in time and Lade became a hill. The environment that made the port eventually unmade it.
entries.note: Helmut Brückner et al., geoarchaeological studies of the Maeander delta (1990s–2000s).

entries.label: The first coins
entries.hint: A foundation deposit under the early Artemision held lumps and electrum coins stamped with a lion's head or striped marks, among the earliest coins known, minted in natural gold-silver alloy from the Pactolus. A stater inscribed 'I am the badge of Phanes' is one of the first coins with a name, its exact origin in Ionia or Caria debated. The coin was a Lydian-Ionian invention and spread fast.
entries.note: D. G. Hogarth, Excavations at Ephesus: The Archaic Artemisia (1908); Robert Wallace, 'The origin of electrum coinage' (1987); Colin Kraay on archaic coinage.

entries.label: Chian wine
entries.hint: Chios was famed for its wine, and Chian amphorae with their white-slipped bodies are found in Egypt, the Black Sea and Italy. The island's farmers made a cash crop of the grape. By the sixth century Chios was a rich island whose vessels travelled the world.
entries.note: John Boardman and Chian amphora studies; Athenaeus 1.26 on Chian wine.

entries.label: Milesian wool
entries.hint: The sheep of Miletus's countryside were the source of wool that the Greeks counted among the finest, woven and dyed in the city's workshops and sold across the Aegean and the Black Sea. The cloth economy ran on the same sea roads as the city's colonies.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The tunnel of Eupalinos, the marsh foundation of the Artemision, hollow bronze and the Ionic alphabet

entries.label: The Ionic alphabet
entries.hint: The East Greek alphabet used in Ionia, notably at Miletus, dropped the old letter for 'h' to mark long vowels: eta for the long e and omega for the long o. Athens adopted this Ionic alphabet officially in 403 BC, and it became the standard Greek one.
entries.note: Lilian Jeffery, The Local Scripts of Archaic Greece (1961).

entries.label: Hollow-cast bronze
entries.hint: Rhoikos and Theodoros of Samos were credited with the invention of casting hollow bronze statues, using a clay core and the lost-wax method. The technique made larger figures possible at lower cost and shaped Greek bronze sculpture from then on.

entries.label: A temple on a marsh
entries.hint: The builders of the great Artemision, Chersiphron and his son Metagenes, chose a marshy site for protection from earthquakes and, as Pliny tells it, laid its foundation on layers of charcoal and fleeces. Architraves were raised on ramps of sandbags. The temple was among the Seven Wonders.

entries.label: The tunnel of Eupalinos
entries.hint: Under Polycrates, the engineer Eupalinos of Megara drove a tunnel more than a kilometre long through Mount Kastro to bring water to the city, working from both ends, and the two teams met within a few metres. It is the earliest tunnel known to have been dug from both ends with surveying, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
entries.note: Herodotus 3.60; June Goodfield and Stephen Toulmin on the tunnel's surveying (1965); UNESCO listing (1992).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Milesian colonies on the Black Sea, the Hellenion at Naukratis, Phocaea's western voyages and the mercenaries of Egypt

entries.label: Miletus and the Black Sea
entries.hint: From the seventh century Miletus planted colonies on the Hellespont, the Propontis and the Black Sea — Abydos, Cyzicus, Sinope, Istros, Olbia, Panticapaeum — so that later writers credited it with some ninety. The Black Sea became a Greek lake for grain, fish, timber and slaves, and the city kept its ties with its daughters.
entries.note: Pliny, Natural History 5.112; Strabo 14.1.6; Alan Ivantchik and Gocha Tsetskhladze on the Black Sea colonies.

entries.label: Greek and Carian mercenaries in Egypt
entries.hint: Psamtik I took Ionian and Carian pirates into the Egyptian army, after a dream of 'bronze men from the sea'. Under Psamtik II, a force of Greeks and Carians scratched their names on the colossi at Abu Simbel when the army marched into Nubia. Ionians were at once soldiers and traders.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.152, 2.163; Abu Simbel Greek graffito (Meiggs and Lewis no. 7).

entries.label: The Greek port in Egypt
entries.hint: At Naukratis in the Nile Delta, the Pharaoh allowed Greek traders to settle. Ionian cities — Chios, Teos, Phocaea, Clazomenae — joined others in a common sanctuary, the Hellenion, while Miletus, Samos and Aegina had their own. The port brought Egyptian stone-working, faience and ideas into Greek life.
entries.note: Herodotus 2.178–179; Alan Johnston and Alexandra Villing on Naukratis.

entries.label: Phocaea's voyages to the west
entries.hint: The Phocaeans were the first Greeks to make long voyages, in fifty-oared galleys, to the Adriatic, Etruria, Iberia and Tartessos, where the king Arganthonius is said to have offered them silver for a city wall. They founded Massalia (Marseille) about 600 BC and Alalia on Corsica about 565 BC.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A mixed foundation, the Lydian and Persian overlords and the end of Ionian independence

entries.label: A mixed foundation
entries.hint: The Greek settlers found Carians, Lelegians and Luwian speakers on the coast; Herodotus says that most of the Ionian cities took Carian wives and had kings from Lycia and Messenia, so that Ionians were of mixed descent. Late Bronze Age Millawanda (Miletus) had been a Mycenaean outpost. The Ionian identity was constructed on top of an older population.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.146–147; Hittite letters on Millawanda (Tawagalawa letter, CTH 181).

entries.label: From Lydian to Persian overlords
entries.hint: The Lydian kings made the Greek cities of the coast tributary to Sardis for the first time and with the fall of Croesus the Persian Empire took over the same system. For two centuries the Ionians were subjects of a land power, with every turn of Persian policy felt on the coast.

entries.label: The end of Ionian independence
entries.hint: Lade and the fall of Miletus ended the Ionian cities' effective independence and put an end to Miletus's age of greatness; Athens's support of the revolt became a reason for Persia's invasion of Greece in 490 BC. The Ionians would be free again only after the Persian defeats of 479.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The oath of the Milesian wives, the eunuch-dealer of Chios and the captive Milesians on the Tigris

entries.label: The oath of the Milesian wives
entries.hint: Herodotus says that the Ionian founders of Miletus killed the Carian men and married their women, who made an oath, passed to their daughters, never to eat with their husbands or to call them by name. Whether the story is more than legend is not known, but it records a memory of a conquest where women were the spoils and carried their own customs into the new city.

entries.label: The eunuch-dealer of Chios
entries.hint: Chios was said to be the first Greek city to buy slaves and Panionius of Chios made his living by acquiring good-looking boys, castrating them and selling them at Sardis and Ephesus as eunuchs, to be had at the highest price in Persian courts. One of his victims, Hermotimus, in time took his revenge.

entries.label: The Milesians on the Tigris
entries.hint: Darius spared the surviving Milesians from massacre and settled them at Ampe on the Persian Gulf near the mouth of the Tigris, giving their land to the Persians and the Carians. The city's people lost both home and name. Their descendants lived out their lives in Mesopotamia.
